claim: Spatial patterns in genetic diversity are shaped by individuals dispersing from their parents and larger-scale population movements.
source: Spatial patterns in genetic diversity are shaped by individuals dispersing from their parents and larger-scale population movements.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in spatial population genetics, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: Patterns of movement shape the underlying genealogies along the genome leading to geographic patterns of isolation-by-distance in contemporary population genetic data.
source: It has long been appreciated that these patterns of movement shape the underlying genealogies along the genome leading to geographic patterns of isolation-by-distance in contemporary population genetic data.
evidence: This statement references long-standing theoretical understanding in population genetics.

claim: Extracting information contained in genealogies along recombining sequences has, until recently, not been computationally feasible.
source: However, extracting the enormous amount of information contained in genealogies along recombining sequences has, until recently, not been computationally feasible.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical state of computational methods in the field.

claim: The method uses thousands of trees to estimate per-generation dispersal rates.
source: Here, we capitalize on important recent advances in genome-wide gene-genealogy reconstruction and develop methods to use thousands of trees to estimate per-generation dispersal rates and to locate the genetic ancestors of a sample back through time.
evidence: This describes the methodology developed in the study.

claim: The method can locate genetic ancestors of a sample back through time.
source: Here, we capitalize on important recent advances in genome-wide gene-genealogy reconstruction and develop methods to use thousands of trees to estimate per-generation dispersal rates and to locate the genetic ancestors of a sample back through time.
evidence: This describes the methodology developed in the study.

claim: The method takes a likelihood approach in continuous space using branching Brownian motion as a prior distribution of spatial genealogies.
source: We take a likelihood approach in continuous space using a simple approximate model (branching Brownian motion) as our prior distribution of spatial genealogies.
evidence: This describes the statistical framework of the method.

claim: The dispersal rate in Arabidopsis thaliana is estimated to be roughly 60 km²/generation.
source: We estimate a dispersal rate of roughly 60 km2/generation, slightly higher across latitude than across longitude, potentially reflecting a northward post-glacial expansion.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying the method to A. thaliana data.

claim: Dispersal in Arabidopsis thaliana is slightly higher across latitude than across longitude.
source: We estimate a dispersal rate of roughly 60 km2/generation, slightly higher across latitude than across longitude, potentially reflecting a northward post-glacial expansion.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying the method to A. thaliana data.

claim: Higher latitudinal dispersal in Arabidopsis thaliana potentially reflects a northward post-glacial expansion.
source: We estimate a dispersal rate of roughly 60 km2/generation, slightly higher across latitude than across longitude, potentially reflecting a northward post-glacial expansion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dispersal rate results in the context of known biogeographic history.

claim: Large-scale movements of different peoples across the world have been learned from ancient DNA in the past decade.
source: For example, in the past decade we have learnt about the large-scale movement of different peoples across the world from ancient DNA (Slatkin and Racimo, 2016; Reich, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Large-scale movements of individuals occur in other species during biological invasions or with the retreat and expansion of populations in and out of glacial refugia.
source: Such large-scale movements of individuals also occur in other species during biological invasions or with the retreat and expansion of populations in and out of glacial refugia, tracking the waxing and waning of the ice ages (Hewitt, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: An individual's set of genealogical ancestors expands rapidly geographically back through time in sexually reproducing organisms.
source: An individual's set of genealogical ancestors expands rapidly geographically back through time in sexually reproducing organisms (Kelleher et al., 2016b; Coop, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: More than a few tens of generations back, an individual's genetic ancestors represent only a tiny sample of their vast number of genealogical ancestors due to limited recombination each generation.
source: Due to limited recombination each generation, more than a few tens of generations back an individual's genetic ancestors represent only a tiny sample of their vast number of genealogical ancestors (Donnelly, 1983; Coop, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Individuals who are geographically close are often genetically more similar across their genomes because their ancestral lineages have only dispersed for a relatively short time and distance since they last shared a geographically close common ancestor.
source: We can hope to learn about the geography of genetic ancestors because individuals who are geographically close are often genetically more similar across their genomes; their ancestral lineages have only dispersed for a relatively short time and distance since they last shared a geographically close common ancestor.
evidence: This describes the theoretical basis for isolation-by-distance.

claim: The pattern of geographically close individuals being genetically more similar is termed isolation-by-distance.
source: This pattern is termed isolation-by-distance.
evidence: This is a definition of a well-established concept in population genetics.

claim: Ideas about the effects of geography and genealogy have underlain understanding of spatial population genetics since its inception.
source: These ideas about the effects of geography and genealogy have underlain our understanding of spatial population genetics since its inception (Wright, 1943; Malécot, 1948).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: Under coalescent models, lineages move spatially as a Brownian motion if dispersal is random and local.
source: Under coalescent models, lineages move spatially, as a Brownian motion if dispersal is random and local, splitting to give rise to descendent lineages until we reach the present day.
evidence: This describes a theoretical model in spatial population genetics.

claim: Spatial genealogy models are the basis of methods that seek violations of isolation-by-distance.
source: These models also are the basis of methods that seek violations of isolation-by-distance (Wang and Bradburd, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: With few exceptions, spatial genealogies have not proven useful for inferences because we have not been able to construct these genealogies along recombining sequences.
source: While spatial genealogies have proven incredibly useful for theoretical tools and intuition, with few exceptions they have not proven useful for inferences because we have not been able to construct these genealogies along recombining sequences.
evidence: This describes a historical limitation in the field.

claim: In non-recombining chromosomes (e.g., mtDNA and Y), constructed genealogies have successfully been used to understand patterns of dispersal and spatial spread.
source: In non-recombining chromosomes (e.g., mtDNA and Y), constructed genealogies have successfully been used to understand patterns of dispersal and spatial spread (Avise, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Spatial genealogy inferences from non-recombining chromosomes are necessarily limited as a single genealogy holds only limited information about the history of populations in a recombining species.
source: However, these spatial genealogy inferences are necessarily limited as a single genealogy holds only limited information about the history of populations in a recombining species (Barton and Wilson, 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Phylogenetic approaches to geography have been more widely and successfully applied to pathogens to track the spatial spread of epidemics, such as SARS-CoV-2.
source: Phylogenetic approaches to geography 'phylogeography'; Knowles, 2009 have been more widely and successfully applied to pathogens to track the spatial spread of epidemics, such as SARS-CoV-2 (Martin et al., 2021), but such approaches have yet to be applied to the thousands of genealogical trees that exist in sexual populations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Recent advances have enabled the ability to infer a sequence of genealogies, with branch lengths, across recombining genomes.
source: Here, we capitalize on the recent ability to infer a sequence of genealogies, with branch lengths, across recombining genomes (Rasmussen et al., 2014; Speidel et al., 2019; Wohns et al., 2021; Schaefer et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2023; Gunnarsson et al., 2024; Deng et al., 2024, reviewed in Wong et al., 2024; Lewanski et al., 2024; Nielsen et al., 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: The method uses a sequence of trees to estimate dispersal rates and locate genetic ancestors in continuous, two-dimensional space under the assumption of Brownian motion.
source: Equipped with this information, we develop a method that uses a sequence of trees to estimate dispersal rates and locate genetic ancestors in continuous, two-dimensional space under the assumption of Brownian motion.
evidence: This describes the methodology developed in the study.

claim: The method uses thousands of approximately unlinked trees to multiply likelihoods across trees to get a genome-wide estimate of dispersal rate.
source: Using thousands of approximately unlinked trees, we multiply likelihoods of the dispersal rate across trees to get a genome-wide estimate and use the sequence of trees to predict a cloud of ancestral locations as a way to visualize geographic ancestries.
evidence: This describes the methodology developed in the study.

claim: The method uses the sequence of trees to predict a cloud of ancestral locations as a way to visualize geographic ancestries.
source: Using thousands of approximately unlinked trees, we multiply likelihoods of the dispersal rate across trees to get a genome-wide estimate and use the sequence of trees to predict a cloud of ancestral locations as a way to visualize geographic ancestries.
evidence: This describes the methodology developed in the study.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana is a species with a wide geographic distribution and a complex history.
source: We first test our approach with simulations and then apply it to Arabidopsis thaliana, a species with a wide geographic distribution and a complex history (Fulgione and Hancock, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Lineages covary in their locations because of shared evolutionary histories – lineages with a more recent common ancestor covary more.
source: Lineages covary in their locations because of shared evolutionary histories – lineages with a more recent common ancestor covary more.
evidence: This describes a theoretical property of the model.

claim: Any point along a tree at any locus is a genetic ancestor of one or more current day samples.
source: Any point along a tree at any locus is a genetic ancestor of one or more current day samples.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about genetic ancestry.

claim: Under the model, the location of an ancestor is influenced by the locations of all samples in the same tree, including those that are not direct descendants.
source: Under this model, the location of an ancestor is influenced by the locations of all samples in the same tree, including those that are not direct descendants (cf. Wohns et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes a property of the model with a citation for comparison.

claim: The method estimates marginal trees along the genome using Relate.
source: We estimate marginal trees along the genome using Relate (Speidel et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the computational tool used in the study.

claim: Relate infers a sequence of tree topologies and associated branch lengths, and can return a set of posterior draws of the branch lengths on a given tree.
source: Relate infers a sequence of tree topologies and associated branch lengths, and can return a set of posterior draws of the branch lengths on a given tree (it was the only method that did so for a large number of samples when we began this work, but now see Wohns et al., 2021; Deng et al., 2024).
evidence: This describes the capabilities of the Relate software with citations to other methods.

claim: Relate gives a posterior distribution of branch lengths that is estimated using a coalescent prior, which assumes a panmictic population of varying population size.
source: Relate gives us a posterior distribution of branch lengths that is estimated using a coalescent prior, which assumes a panmictic population of varying population size (the size changes are estimated as part of the method), where any two lineages are equally likely to coalesce.
evidence: This describes the assumptions of the Relate software.

claim: The panmictic prior results in a bias in the coalescent times under a spatial model, where geographically proximate samples are more likely to coalesce.
source: This panmictic prior results in a bias in the coalescent times under a spatial model, where geographically proximate samples are more likely to coalesce.
evidence: This describes a source of bias in the inference method.

claim: The method uses importance sampling to correct for the bias from the panmictic prior.
source: To correct for this bias we make use of importance sampling to weight the samples of branch lengths at each locus.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach to address bias.

claim: The method concentrates on the recent past history of the sample for estimates of dispersal rates.
source: In practice, we concentrate on the recent past history of our sample. For our estimates of dispersal rates in particular we do not want to assume that our model of Gaussian dispersal (and branching Brownian motion) holds deep into the past history of the sample.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the study.

claim: Long-term movement of lineages is constrained by geographic barriers (e.g., oceans) and larger-scale population movements may erase geographic signals over deep time scales.
source: This is because the long-term movement of lineages is constrained by geographic barriers (e.g., oceans) and larger-scale population movements may erase geographic signals over deep time scales.
evidence: This describes a rationale for focusing on recent history.

claim: In a finite habitat the locations of coalescence events further back in time become independent of sampling locations as lineages have moved around sufficiently.
source: On a theoretical level ignoring the deep past may also be justified because in a finite habitat the locations of coalescence events further back in time become independent of sampling locations as lineages have moved around sufficiently (Wilkins and Wakeley, 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Branching Brownian motion, also known as the Brownian–Yule process, is a simple model of spatial genealogies in a continuous population.
source: Branching Brownian motion, also known as the Brownian–Yule process, is a simple model of spatial genealogies in a continuous population (Malécot, 1948; Wright, 1943).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to foundational work.

claim: The lack of local density dependence in branching Brownian motion generates non-uniform population density.
source: This simplicity comes at a cost: the lack of local density dependence generates non-uniform population density (Felsenstein, 1975) and the assumption of unbounded space overestimates the distance between samples (Kalkauskas et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The assumption of unbounded space in branching Brownian motion overestimates the distance between samples.
source: This simplicity comes at a cost: the lack of local density dependence generates non-uniform population density (Felsenstein, 1975) and the assumption of unbounded space overestimates the distance between samples (Kalkauskas et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: More complex models, such as the spatial Lambda Fleming–Viot process, overcome the issues of branching Brownian motion but are computationally expensive for inference.
source: More complex models, such as the spatial Lambda Fleming–Viot process (Barton et al., 2010), overcome these issues and more, but are computationally expensive for inference (Wirtz and Guindon, 2024).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Branching Brownian motion remains an analytically tractable model and a reasonable approximation over short-time scales.
source: Branching Brownian motion remains an analytically tractable model and a reasonable approximation over short-time scales (Edwards, 1970; Rannala and Yang, 1996; Meligkotsidou and Fearnhead, 2007; Novembre and Slatkin, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The method systematically underestimates simulated dispersal rates.
source: Our method systematically underestimates simulated dispersal rates (Figure 2A), as expected given that our simple unbounded Brownian motion model allows the samples to be more broadly distributed than the finite habitat (e.g., Ianni-Ravn et al., 2023; Kalkauskas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a result from simulation tests shown in Figure 2A, with citations explaining the expected bias.

claim: The dispersal rate inferred from the true trees can be interpreted as a true 'effective' dispersal rate given the habitat boundaries, local competition, etc.
source: Despite the fact that we tend to underestimate the simulated dispersal rate, our estimates are highly correlated with the simulated values and we can interpret the dispersal rate inferred from the true trees as a true 'effective' dispersal rate given the habitat boundaries, local competition, etc.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: The dispersal estimates from the inferred trees are highly correlated with those from the true trees, with a slight upward bias.
source: Encouragingly, the dispersal estimates from the inferred trees are highly correlated with those from the true trees, with a slight upward bias.
evidence: This is a result from simulation tests.

claim: The upward bias in dispersal estimates from inferred trees can be explained by isolation-by-distance and errors in inferred tree topologies, causing geographically more distant samples to be mistakenly inferred as closer relatives.
source: This upward bias can be explained by isolation-by-distance and errors in inferred tree topologies, causing geographically more distant samples to be mistakenly inferred as closer relatives.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the bias observed in simulation results.

claim: The upward bias in dispersal estimates may result from Relate tending to underestimate longer coalescence times.
source: The upward bias may also result from Relate tending to underestimate longer coalescence times (Y C Brandt et al., 2022), which is consistent with the bias decreasing at smaller cutoff times.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to published work.

claim: The bias in dispersal estimates decreases as fewer trees are sampled at each locus.
source: The bias increases as we use sample fewer trees at each locus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), showing that our spatial prior implemented via importance sampling improves our inference.
evidence: This is a result from simulation tests shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Sampling more individuals reduces noise across replicates but can actually increase bias in dispersal estimates.
source: Sampling more individuals reduces noise across replicates but can actually increase bias (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), perhaps because of a greater chance of an error when inferring a larger tree.
evidence: This is a result from simulation tests shown in a supplementary figure, with speculation about the cause.

claim: The 95% confidence ellipses generally do a good job of capturing true ancestral locations at individual loci.
source: While the ellipses generally do a good job of capturing true ancestral locations (the 'x's), the size of an ellipse at any one locus grows relatively rapidly as we move back in time, meaning that at deeper times (or higher dispersal rates) any one locus contains little information about an ancestor's location (as is the case for ancestral state reconstruction in phylogenetics; Schluter et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a result from simulation tests with a citation for comparison.

claim: The size of confidence ellipses for ancestral locations grows relatively rapidly as we move back in time.
source: While the ellipses generally do a good job of capturing true ancestral locations (the 'x's), the size of an ellipse at any one locus grows relatively rapidly as we move back in time, meaning that at deeper times (or higher dispersal rates) any one locus contains little information about an ancestor's location (as is the case for ancestral state reconstruction in phylogenetics; Schluter et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a result from simulation tests with a citation for comparison.

claim: The method outperforms straw-man estimates (current location of each sample and the mean location across samples) for locating ancestors.
source: While our method outperforms the straw-man estimates, the mean squared error in our inferred location of the ancestor at a locus grows relatively rapidly back in time, as expected under Brownian motion.
evidence: This is a result from simulation tests comparing different methods.

claim: The genome-wide mean of the MLE locations remains closer to the true mean location of genetic ancestors than at any one locus, even with the inferred trees.
source: The genome-wide mean of the MLE locations remains closer to the true mean location of genetic ancestors (Figure 2E) than at any one locus, even with the inferred trees, suggesting our method can successfully trace major trends in the geographic ancestry of a sample deeper into the past.
evidence: This is a result from simulation tests shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The error in ancestral locations appears relatively robust to the number of trees sampled per locus.
source: In contrast to dispersal, the error in ancestral locations appears relatively robust to the number of trees sampled per locus (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) and the number of samples (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a result from simulation tests shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana has a complex, and not yet fully resolved, spatial history.
source: A. thaliana has a complex, and not yet fully resolved, spatial history (Fulgione and Hancock, 2018; Hsu et al., 2019), including range expansions, admixture between multiple glacial refugia, and long-distance colonization.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The dispersal rates estimated from the 1135 A. thaliana accessions dataset were unreasonably large, on the order of 10^4 km²/generation.
source: Unfortunately, the dispersal rates we estimated from this data were unreasonably large, on the order of 104 km2/generation, even after removing pairs of near-identical samples and geographic outliers (for more details see our preprint, Osmond and Coop, 2021).
evidence: This is a result from applying the method to a specific dataset.

claim: The very high dispersal rate estimates from the 1135 and 1500 individual datasets are an artefact of long runs of identity between pairs of geographically separated sequences.
source: The very high dispersal rate estimates from these datasets is an artefact of long runs of identity between pairs of geographically separated sequences (see Figure S6 of Osmond and Coop, 2021).
evidence: This is an interpretation of problematic results with reference to a figure in a preprint.

claim: The stretches of identity in the large A. thaliana datasets result from the incorrect imputation of missing genotypes.
source: We believe that these stretches of identity result from the incorrect imputation of missing genotypes, a problem that could not be resolved through various data filters.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the cause of the problematic results.

claim: Imputation can obscure rare alleles, which artificially lowers the divergence between similar sequences, lowers coalescence times, and biases dispersal estimates upward.
source: However, imputation can obscure rare alleles, which artificially lowers the divergence between similar sequences. This lowers coalescence times and biases dispersal estimates upward.
evidence: This is an explanation of how imputation affects the results.

claim: The issue with imputation was resolved by analysing a smaller dataset with 66 long-read genomes where imputation could be avoided.
source: We resolved this issue by analysing a smaller dataset with 66 long-read genomes (Wlodzimierz et al., 2023), where we could avoid imputing and capture more genetic variation (Igolkina et al., 2024) and therefore be much more confident in the resulting genealogies.
evidence: This describes the solution to the data quality problem, with citations.

claim: Arabidopsis thaliana is a selfer with a relatively low rate of outcrossing.
source: A. thaliana is a selfer with a relatively low rate of outcrossing (Bomblies et al., 2010; Platt et al., 2010), thus it is worth taking a moment to consider the impact of selfing on our inferences.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Linkage disequilibrium breaks down relatively rapidly in A. thaliana, on the scales of tens of kilobases.
source: However, in practice, linkage disequilibrium breaks down relatively rapidly in A. thaliana, on the scales of tens of kilobases (Kim et al., 2007), such that many trees along the genome should have relatively independent genealogies.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Individuals with recent inbreeding (selfing) in their family tree will have fewer genealogical and genetic ancestors than outbred individuals.
source: A related issue is that the individuals with recent inbreeding (selfing) in their family tree will have fewer genealogical and genetic ancestors than outbred individuals.
evidence: This is a theoretical consequence of selfing.

claim: Even with relatively low rates of outbreeding the number of ancestors still grows rapidly in selfing populations.
source: Thus in any recent time-slice there are a reduced number of independent genetic ancestors of a individual from a selfing population, but even with relatively low rates of outbreeding the number of ancestors still grows rapidly (Lachance, 2009), meaning that many trees along the genome should have relatively independent spatial histories.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Relate uses a mutational clock to estimate branch lengths, and thus they should be well calibrated to a generational time scale.
source: Finally, while the effective recombination rate may vary through time along with rates of selfing, Relate uses a mutational clock to estimate branch lengths, and thus they should be well calibrated to a generational time scale.
evidence: This describes a property of the Relate software.

claim: Using the full trees, back to the most recent common ancestor of each, the dispersal rate in A. thaliana is estimated to be about 30 km²/generation.
source: Using the full trees, back to the most recent common ancestor of each, we estimate a dispersal rate of about 30 km2/generation.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying the method to A. thaliana data.

claim: Using the harmonic mean pairwise coalescent time over trees gives a dispersal rate estimate of roughly 40 km²/generation.
source: Using instead the harmonic mean pairwise coalescent time over trees, we estimate a dispersal rate of roughly 40 km2/generation, similar to our estimate.
evidence: This is a result from an alternative estimation approach.

claim: With cutoffs of 10^5 and 10^4 generations, the estimated dispersal rate in A. thaliana increases to about 35 and 60 km²/generation, respectively.
source: With cutoffs of 105 and 104, the estimated dispersal rate increases to about 35 and 60 km2/generation, respectively, which we believe is because finite habitat boundaries lower the effective dispersal rate over longer time scales but also suggests faster rates of lineage movement post-glaciation, for example, due to a recent northward range expansion.
evidence: This is a quantitative result with interpretation.

claim: The dispersal rate estimates from the A. thaliana data are considerably higher than a recent estimate using machine learning directly on genotype data, which was on the order of 1 km²/generation.
source: These dispersal estimates are considerably higher than a recent estimate, using machine learning directly on genotype data, that was on the order of 1 km2/generation (Smith et al., 2023).
evidence: This is a comparison with results from another study.

claim: The lower dispersal estimate from Smith et al. (2023) likely more strongly reflects shorter-term local dispersal, while the current study's estimate strikes a balance between slower recent movements and faster movements that have occasionally occurred in deeper time.
source: This previous study used a similar sample size but a much narrower geographic range of more closely related individuals. It is therefore likely that this lower estimate more strongly reflects shorter-term local dispersal, while we are striking a balance between these slower recent movements and faster movements that have occasionally occurred in deeper time.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the current results with another study.

claim: 'Non-relict' lineages in A. thaliana are proposed to have dispersed from the Black Sea to the Atlantic Ocean (about 2500 km) in the past 10^4 generations.
source: To get a sense of how large a dispersal rate we should expect, 'non-relict' lineages are proposed to have dispersed from the Black Sea to the Atlantic Ocean (about 2500 km) in the past 104 generations (Lee et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The effective dispersal rate estimated for A. thaliana is reasonable given the Brownian motion model and hypothesized movements.
source: We therefore think our effective dispersal rate is a reasonable one given the Brownian motion model and hypothesized movements in A. thaliana.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dispersal rate results.

claim: Dispersal in A. thaliana is estimated to be slightly faster along latitude than along longitude, especially in the past 10^4 generations.
source: We estimate slightly faster dispersal along latitude than along longitude, especially in the past 104 generations.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from applying the method to A. thaliana data.

claim: Faster dispersal along latitude in the past 10^4 generations is consistent with rapid post-glacial expansion in A. thaliana.
source: Faster dispersal along latitude in the past 104 generations is consistent with rapid post-glacial expansion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the dispersal rate results.

claim: Previous studies have emphasized a rapid westward expansion of the non-relict lineages from an eastern glacial refugium in A. thaliana.
source: Previous studies have instead emphasized a rapid westward expansion of the non-relict lineages from an eastern glacial refugium, facilitated by relatively weak environmental gradients and, potentially, human movements and disturbance (1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016; Lee et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The longitudinal dispersal estimate in A. thaliana would possibly increase substantially if non-relict samples from further east were included.
source: It is possible that our longitudinal dispersal estimate would increase substantially if we included non-relict samples from further east.
evidence: This is speculation about how sampling might affect the results.

claim: Consistent with a rapid recent expansion of the non-relict ancestry, lineages from the 'Eurasian' principle component group move relatively quickly towards each other when looking backwards in time.
source: Consistent with a rapid recent expansion of the non-relict ancestry (Lee et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2019), lineages from the 'Eurasian' principle component group (hereafter, non-relicts) move relatively quickly towards each other when looking backwards in time, a visual display of their rapid coalescence over wide geographic distances.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ancestral location results with citations.

claim: The rapid geographic expansion of non-relict ancestry in A. thaliana is especially pronounced further north.
source: Looking forward through time (i.e., reversing the direction of the arrows), this rapid geographic expansion of non-relict ancestry is especially pronounced further north, as might be expected with retreating glaciers and more recent human disturbance (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ancestral location results with a citation.

claim: The non-relict lineages in A. thaliana are all pulled towards the bulk of non-relict samples in southern France, highlighting the limitations of sampling and methods based on contemporary data alone.
source: The fact that the non-relict lineages are all pulled towards the bulk of non-relict samples, in southern France, highlights the limitations of sampling and methods based on contemporary data alone.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ancestral location results.

claim: The non-relicts in A. thaliana likely spread from further east, with a refugium perhaps near the Black Sea.
source: The non-relicts likely spread from further east, with a refugium perhaps near the Black Sea (Lee et al., 2017; Hsu et al., 2019), but this dataset does not have enough samples in that area to infer this.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to published work and acknowledges a limitation of the current dataset.

claim: Nearly all lineages from the 'Iberian relict' principle component group move relatively little, and towards themselves rather than towards the non-relict ancestors.
source: Meanwhile nearly all lineages from the 'Iberian relict' principle component group (hereafter, Iberian relicts) move relatively little, and towards themselves rather than towards the non-relict ancestors.
evidence: This is a result from the ancestral location analysis.

claim: The movement pattern of Iberian relicts is a visual representation of the fact that much of the ancestry of these Iberian relicts has a very different geographic history than much of the non-relicts' ancestry.
source: This is a visual representation of the fact that much of the ancestry of these Iberian relicts has a very different geographic history than much of the non-relicts' ancestry (1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016; Fulgione and Hancock, 2018).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ancestral location results with citations.

claim: Iberian relicts Met-6 and Evs-12 have mean displacements that are much more typical of a non-relict.
source: There are, however, two exceptions, with Iberian relicts Met-6 and Evs-12 having (overlapping) mean displacements that are much more typical of a non-relict.
evidence: This is a result from the ancestral location analysis.

claim: Lineages from the 'non-Iberian relict' principle component group move towards the other samples, slightly more towards the Iberian relicts than the non-relicts.
source: Finally, we see that lineages from the 'non-Iberian relict' principle component group (hereafter, non-Iberian relicts) move towards the other samples, slightly more towards the Iberian relicts than the non-relicts.
evidence: This is a result from the ancestral location analysis.

claim: The movement of non-Iberian relict lineages is relatively slow, emphasizing the known deep divergence of each of these samples with any other.
source: This movement is, however, relatively slow, emphasizing the known deep divergence of each of these samples with any other (1001 Genomes Consortium, 2016; Fulgione et al., 2018; Fulgione and Hancock, 2018; Fulgione et al., 2022).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ancestral location results with citations.

claim: The ancestors of the non-relict sample 9883 are nearly all located to the northeast, as expected given the locations of the other non-relict samples and the proposed expansion from the east.
source: The first is a typical non-relict (9883) whose ancestors are nearly all located to the northeast, as expected given the locations of the other non-relict samples and the proposed expansion from the east.
evidence: This is a result from the ancestral location analysis with interpretation.

claim: The Iberian relict sample Hum-2 has ancestors mostly located just to the south of it, near the centre of the Iberian relict samples, as expected given the divergence between non-relicts and relicts and the longer history of relicts in the region.
